title: Curriculum leadership: the spotlight and the guardian
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that primary curriculum leadership belongs to senior leaders and the headteacher because it requires an overview of every subject at once. He names two roles. The spotlight directs the whole staff's limited attention to one subject at a time so that colleagues are not overloaded by competing requests from enthusiastic subject leaders. The guardian protects the curriculum as a coherent whole when teachers suggest changes based only on their own units. Subjects out of the spotlight are not idle; their leaders can check coverage, study pupils' work, build subject knowledge and prepare for their turn. The piece is a short practical framework rather than a research-based argument, and its examples (Shang currency, a geography unit ending in non-fiction writing) are illustrative rather than evidenced.
points: Because staff attention is finite, a senior leader should choose which subject gets collective focus at a given time rather than letting every subject leader compete for it.

Subjects waiting outside the spotlight still have useful work: checking coverage against the national curriculum, studying the work of the least advantaged pupils and preparing a sequence of review sessions.

The guardian role exists because a change that looks harmless inside one unit, such as dropping early currency from the Shang dynasty, can leave a gap in a concept like trade across all of key stage 2.
The guardian also protects subject specificity, for example by making sure a cross-curricular writing task at the end of a geography unit is framed as writing and not mistaken for geography.
Checklists can help subject leaders build a mental model of what makes a strong curriculum in their subject.
quotes: If we try and pay attention to too much at once, nothing will be done in any sufficient depth.

But if multiple subject leaders do this, colleagues will soon reach overload and have to make their own decisions about what they should pay attention to. And those decisions might be based on their own preferences or their relationships with the subject leaders rather than what is actually a school priority.
Controlling the spotlight involves knowing when a subject needs our collective attention and preparing subject leaders for when the spotlight settles on their subject.
No curriculum survives first contact with the reality of teaching it and getting children to understand and learn it. Improvements to any curriculum are to be expected.
Teachers making changes based only on their own experiences risks the coherence of a curriculum and therefore an important role of a senior leaders is to be the guardian. The guardian of coherence.
There is always a risk of curriculum choices being adapted that dilute subject specificity.

The suggested task is writing, not necessarily Geography. The discipline of Geography might include explaining a human or physical process but there can be a subtle difference in purpose between this and a writing a non fiction piece geared towards applying what children have learned in the writing curriculum.
